introduction-demystifying-the-magic.core: Git is a content-addressed database of snapshots, plus movable name tags pointing into it. Once you understand that model, no Git state is scary.

first_principles.problem: Developers memorise commands and panic at a detached HEAD or a messy merge because they don't know what Git actually did.
truths: Every Git command manipulates objects or pointers.
Nothing committed is easily lost.
Understanding the model beats memorising commands.
derivation: Then merges, rebase, bisect and reflog follow naturally.

analogy.title: Learning how an engine works
analogy.story: A driver who knows the engine can diagnose the strange noise instead of being stranded.
analogy.breaks: You don't need every byte-level detail, just the model.

example.title: Detached HEAD panic
flow: HEAD points at a commit, not a branch
New commits have no branch name

steps.label: Insight
steps.detail: Nothing is broken; a pointer is simply not attached to a branch.

example.outcome: Git errors turn into readable states.

check.q: What is a detached HEAD in model terms?
check.a: HEAD pointing directly at a commit instead of at a branch ref.

the-object-model-gits-key-value-database.core: Git stores four object types (blob, tree, commit, tag) in `.git/objects`, each addressed by the hash of its content. Identical content is stored only once.

first_principles.problem: Without a model, it's mysterious how Git deduplicates files, detects corruption, or knows what changed.
truths: The same content always produces the same hash.
Content-addressing makes data tamper-evident.
Directories can be represented as lists of names → hashes.
derivation: **Tree** = a directory listing of names → blob or tree hashes.
**Commit** = a tree plus parent(s), author and message.
**Tag** = an annotated pointer to an object.

analogy.title: A library catalogue by fingerprint
analogy.story: Every book is shelved by the fingerprint of its text, so two identical copies share a single shelf slot.
analogy.breaks: Git also compresses objects into packfiles with deltas, so storage isn't literally one file per object.

example.title: Inspect an object

steps.label: Insight
steps.detail: Renaming a file adds no new blob, only a new tree entry.

code.text:
git cat-file -t HEAD        # commit
git cat-file -p HEAD^{tree} # tree listing
git hash-object README.md   # blob hash

example.outcome: you can reason about how Git stores data.

check.q: Why doesn't a blob store the filename?
check.a: Names belong to trees, so identical content is stored once regardless of name.

the-commit-object-snapshots-not-diffs.core: A commit records a complete snapshot (a root tree) and links to its parent(s). Diffs are computed on demand by comparing snapshots.

first_principles.problem: Thinking of commits as diffs makes checkout, revert and cherry-pick confusing.
truths: Unchanged files reuse the existing blob hashes.
Parent links form a DAG.
Any two snapshots can be compared.
derivation: Each commit points to a **full tree**.
Unchanged parts **reuse objects**, so it stays cheap.

analogy.title: Photographs, not edit notes
analogy.story: Each commit is a photo of the whole room. To see what moved, you compare two photos.
analogy.breaks: The photos share unchanged pixels (objects), so the album doesn't grow by full copies.

example.title: Checking out an old commit
example.scenario: It's fast because the snapshot is already complete.

steps.label: Insight
steps.detail: Checkout writes that tree to disk; there are no diffs to replay.

code.text:
git cat-file -p HEAD
# tree 9c1f...
# parent a3b4...
# author ...

check.q: Does Git store diffs in commits?
check.a: No. A commit points to a full tree; diffs are computed by comparing trees.

refs-heads-tags-and-remotes.core: A ref is a file containing a commit hash. Branches move as you commit, tags stay fixed, remote-tracking refs mirror the server, and HEAD points to your current branch.

first_principles.problem: Without knowing that branches are just pointers, creating, deleting and resetting them feels dangerous.
truths: Hashes are unreadable to humans.
A pointer is cheap to create and move.
Commits stay in the database even when no ref names them.

analogy.title: Bookmarks in a book
analogy.story: A branch is a bookmark that moves as you read, a tag is a sticky note that stays put, and HEAD is your finger.
analogy.breaks: Deleting a bookmark doesn't tear out pages, but unreferenced commits are eventually garbage-collected.

steps.label: Insight
steps.detail: Creating a branch writes one file, which is why it's instant.

check.q: Why is creating a branch so cheap in Git?
check.a: It's just a small file holding a commit hash.

merging-strategies.core: If the target hasn't moved, a merge just fast-forwards the pointer. If both sides diverged, Git does a three-way merge from their common ancestor and records a merge commit with two parents.

first_principles.problem: Teams are surprised by merge commits, or by their absence, and don't understand where conflicts come from.
truths: The relationship between the histories decides the strategy.
A common ancestor is the reference point for a three-way merge.
Conflicts arise when both sides changed the same lines.
derivation: Target is an **ancestor** of the feature → **fast-forward** (move the pointer).
`--no-ff` forces a merge commit to keep the record.

analogy.title: Merging two edited copies of a document
analogy.story: Compare each copy against the original: take each side's unique edits, and ask a human where both edited the same sentence.
analogy.breaks: Git merges line by line, so it doesn't understand meaning and can't spot semantic conflicts.

example.title: Two scenarios
example.scenario: main unchanged vs main moved on.

steps.label: Insight
steps.detail: The merge base is what makes automatic merging possible.

example.outcome: you can predict how a merge will turn out.

check.a: When the target branch has no commits that aren't already in the source.

interactive-rebase-cleaning-up-history.core: `git rebase -i` replays your local commits so you can squash, reword, reorder or drop them before sharing. Never rewrite commits other people already have.

first_principles.problem: 'wip', 'fix typo' and 'oops' commits clutter the permanent history that everyone reads later.
truths: Rebase creates new commits with new hashes.
Rewriting shared history breaks collaborators.
Clean history helps review and bisect.

analogy.title: Editing a draft before publishing
analogy.story: Combine scattered notes into clear chapters before the book goes to print, never after.
analogy.breaks: Once something is published (pushed and pulled by others), rewriting it causes real damage.

steps.label: Result
steps.detail: Two meaningful commits, ready for review.

code.text:
pick a1 Add retry logic
fixup b2 fix typo
fixup c3 wip
pick d4 Add tests
fixup e5 lint

check.q: Why not rebase a branch others have pulled?
check.a: It replaces commits they have with new ones, causing duplicates and conflicts.

git-bisect-the-binary-search-debugger.core: `git bisect` binary-searches history between a good commit and a bad one, so it finds the commit that introduced a bug in about log₂(N) steps.

first_principles.problem: A bug appeared somewhere in 400 commits, and testing them one by one would take hours.
truths: The bug is either present or absent at each commit.
Binary search halves the range each step.
Tests can be automated.
derivation: Git checks out the **midpoint**; you test it.
Use **`git bisect run ./test.sh`** to fully automate it.

analogy.title: Guess the number, higher or lower
analogy.story: Guessing 1–400 by halving takes at most 9 tries.
analogy.breaks: It needs a reliable test. Flaky tests send the search the wrong way.

steps.label: Result
steps.detail: Git names the first bad commit in about 9 runs.

code.text:
git bisect start BAD_SHA GOOD_SHA
git bisect run ./scripts/login_under_200ms.sh
git bisect reset

check.q: About how many steps does bisect need for 1,000 commits?

the-safety-net-git-reflog.core: The reflog records every position HEAD and your branches have pointed to, so commits 'lost' to a reset, rebase or amend can be recovered.

first_principles.problem: After a bad `reset --hard` or rebase, the commits vanish from git log and people assume the work is gone.
truths: Destructive commands move pointers; they don't delete objects immediately.
Git logs every pointer move locally.
Unreferenced objects survive until garbage collection.
derivation: Run **`git reflog`** to see past HEAD positions.
Find the hash from **before the mistake**.
Act within the expiry window (90 days by default).

analogy.title: A browser's history
analogy.story: Even after you navigate away, the history lets you go back to the page you came from.
analogy.breaks: The reflog is local only. It can't recover work that was never committed, or work that exists only on someone else's machine.

example.title: Undoing a botched rebase
example.scenario: Go back to how it was before.

steps.label: Result
steps.detail: The branch is back exactly as it was before the rebase.

code.text:
git reflog
# e4f5 HEAD@{0}: rebase finished
# 9a8b HEAD@{5}: commit: add feature
git reset --hard HEAD@{5}

example.outcome: committed work is almost never truly lost.

check.q: Can reflog recover changes you never committed?
check.a: No. It only tracks commits that pointers referenced.
